headline: Funding flows. Contracts expand. Launches resume.
deck: This week, funding rounds and contract expansions signal a steady pulse in the space sector.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M for co-orbital security
stories.body: True Anomaly has secured $190 million in a Series C funding round, bringing its valuation to $1.6 billion. The company focuses on co-orbital security and space domain awareness, a timely investment as the DoD increasingly prioritizes these capabilities. This cash influx follows the trend of defense-oriented startups attracting significant capital.
stories.soWhat: True Anomaly's funding highlights that even in a crowded market, defense-related ventures can still draw hefty checks—perhaps investors are finally realizing that space isn't just for satellites anymore.

stories.head: NASA expands SpaceX crew contract amid Boeing delays
stories.body: NASA has decided to add more missions to its commercial crew contract with SpaceX, a move prompted by ongoing delays in Boeing's Starliner certification. This contract expansion is part of a broader strategy to diversify crew transport options, crucial for maintaining a reliable access to the ISS. The specifics of the additional missions remain under wraps, but they underscore NASA's commitment to reducing reliance on a single provider.
stories.soWhat: This is a classic case of risk management in action; when one rocket stumbles, it's prudent to lean on the one that’s already flying—at least until the other one learns to walk.

stories.head: Blue Origin resumes launches after New Glenn investigation
stories.body: Blue Origin has completed its investigation into the New Glenn launch failure and is set to resume launches, a relief for a company that has faced scrutiny over its operational delays. This comes at a critical time as the launch market tightens, with competitors like SpaceX and Astra ramping up their capabilities. The company’s ability to bounce back will be closely watched by both investors and clients alike.
stories.soWhat: Resuming launches is a necessary step for Blue Origin, but it also raises the question: can they maintain momentum, or will they find themselves back in the launch pad waiting room?

watchlist.title: Keep an eye on hypersonic testing delays
watchlist.body: Continued delays in hypersonic glide-vehicle tests could hinder U.S. defense advancements, prompting a closer look at alternative technologies.

watchlist.title: Sierra Space's Dream Chaser progress
watchlist.body: With the Dream Chaser DoD variant passing its critical design review, the next steps will be crucial for its viability in upcoming missions.

watchlist.title: Palantir's TITAN program extension
watchlist.body: The $480 million extension of Palantir's TITAN program suggests ongoing confidence in its ground station capabilities amidst a competitive landscape.

watchlist.title: Arctic policy updates from the EU
watchlist.body: The EU's upcoming Arctic policy revisions could impact future space operations in the region, particularly for companies eyeing commercial opportunities.

talent.statLabel: Week-over-week growth in resumes from primes to Series B/C
talent.head: Talent is leaving big-aero — and it's not about money
talent.body: Compensation is not the gating factor. The complaint, almost universally, is schedule risk — the inability to ship anything quickly, the half-decade gap between joining and seeing flight hardware, the meeting that exists to schedule the meeting. The startups absorbing this talent will, in two years, be hard to compete with on a level playing field.
